blocks.text: 1. The Input Gate
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742780-198026863.png
The Forget Gate, the previous topic, decided what to discard from the cell state. The Input Gate decides what new information to add to the cell state, explored in full depth throughout this topic.
It is LSTM's second gate, working alongside the forget gate already covered, a genuinely essential complementary mechanism covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping The Preview

This connects back to the quick preview of all three gates, already covered in LSTM Architecture. The input gate was genuinely introduced there as the second of three gates, briefly described in that earlier topic.
This topic genuinely gives it the same complete treatment already given to the forget gate, exploring every mathematical and practical detail already hinted at throughout LSTM Architecture.
3. Two Parts Of The Input Gate

blocks.alt: Two Parts Of The Input Gate
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742780-87365245.png

A genuinely important structural detail connects back to Sigmoid and Tanh, both already covered in the Activation Functions module. The input gate genuinely has two parts: a Sigmoid deciding how much to add, and a Tanh proposing genuinely new candidate values.

This genuinely two-part structure, already covered in this section, directly reuses two activation functions already covered separately in that earlier module, now combined for a genuinely specific new purpose.

blocks.text: 4. The Candidate Values, Explained
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742780-936341142.png

This connects back to Tanh, already covered in the Activation Functions module. The Tanh part genuinely proposes new candidate values that could get added to the cell state, drawing on that earlier activation function.
These are bounded between negative 1 and 1, exactly the range already covered for Tanh in that earlier module, keeping proposed new information genuinely well behaved and consistently scaled.
5. Sigmoid Decides The Amount
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742780-296387040.png

This connects back to the Sigmoid gating mechanism, already covered in LSTM Architecture. The Sigmoid part genuinely decides how much of each candidate value actually gets added, a genuinely direct extension of that earlier gating idea.
This is the exact same 0-to-1 gating idea already covered for the forget gate, applied here to genuinely new information instead of the genuinely existing cell state content.
6. Combining Both Parts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445742781-547246952.png
The genuinely core operation multiplies the Sigmoid output by the Tanh candidate values, element by element, directly combining the two parts already covered in the previous two sections.
This produces the genuinely actual new information that gets added into the cell state, a genuinely direct, concrete result from these two separately covered components working together.

blocks.content: This same multiply-then-combine pattern, already covered in this topic, mirrors the forget gate's own element-wise multiplication already covered in the previous topic, a genuinely consistent design pattern across LSTM's own gates.

blocks.text: 7. Adding To The Cell State
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445743074-370428991.png

This connects back to applying the gate, already covered in The Forget Gate. The cell state genuinely gets updated: forget gate output times old cell state, plus the input gate's own new contribution.
This combines both gates already covered so far into one genuinely complete cell state update, the exact formula already sketched conceptually as the cell state idea back in LSTM Architecture.
8. Why Two Parts Genuinely Makes Sense

A genuinely elegant design insight connects back to the forget gate's own separation of decision from content, already covered. Separating what genuinely could be added, the Tanh part, from how much genuinely should be added, the Sigmoid part.
This mirrors the same genuinely clean separation already covered for the forget gate, just now applied to genuinely adding new information rather than removing old information.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Why The Input Gate Is Genuinely Essential

blocks.alt: Recognizing Why The Input Gate Is Genuinely Essential
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445743074-878909850.png

This connects back to the forget gate alone only removing information, already covered. The input gate, already covered in this topic, is what genuinely lets new, relevant information actually enter the cell state.

This connects back to the cell state idea, already covered in LSTM Architecture, needing both removal and addition. Together with the forget gate, already covered, the input gate completes genuinely active cell state management.
10. Worked Example

The example below directly demonstrates the input gate's own two-part computation, combining Sigmoid and Tanh to produce new information added to the cell state, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

previous_cell_state = np.array([1.0, -0.5, 2.0, 0.3])

# already covered as the two parts of the input gate in this topic
sigmoid_amount = sigmoid(np.array([1.5, -2.0, 0.5, 3.0]))     # how much to add
tanh_candidates = np.tanh(np.array([0.8, 1.2, -0.5, 0.9]))     # what could be added

new_information = sigmoid_amount * tanh_candidates  # already covered as combining both parts in this topic
print(f"Sigmoid amount (how much): {np.round(sigmoid_amount, 3)}")
print(f"Tanh candidates (what could be added): {np.round(tanh_candidates, 3)}")
print(f"New information added: {np.round(new_information, 3)}")

# already covered as adding to the cell state in this topic
forget_gate_output = sigmoid(np.array([2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0]))  # a genuinely mostly-keeping forget gate
new_cell_state = forget_gate_output * previous_cell_state + new_information
print(f"\nNew cell state (forget gate times old, plus new information): {np.round(new_cell_state, 3)}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the input gate's own two parts combining into new information, then that new information genuinely added to the cell state alongside the forget gate's own contribution, exactly the complete update already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: The input gate decides what new information to add to the cell state.
It has two parts: a Sigmoid deciding how much to add, and a Tanh proposing candidate values.
The Tanh candidate values are bounded between negative 1 and 1.
The Sigmoid part decides how much of each candidate value actually gets added.
Multiplying these two parts together produces the actual new information added.
The full cell state update combines the forget gate's output with the input gate's new contribution.
This mirrors the forget gate's own clean separation of content from amount.
Together with the forget gate, it completes active cell state management.
Next up: The Output Gate, deciding what to reveal from the cell state as the hidden state.
